investment_summary:
Microsoft's FY2026 10-K [1] shows strong business momentum. Revenue rose 18% to $331.8 billion, net income rose 31%, and Azure grew 41% [1]. Commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678 billion, up 84% [1].

The AI build-out absorbs much of the gain. Capital expenditure climbed from $64.6 billion to $115.9 billion, and free cash flow fell 6% to $67.0 billion [1][2].

The current enterprise value implies 22.0% annual revenue growth for ten years [3]. That is above the 16.1% historical three-year CAGR and the 19.3% consensus for FY2027 [3]. At that pace the implied return is 6.7% against a 10.1% WACC [3]. Consensus data is dated after the 10-K. The price therefore requires growth above both history and consensus for a decade.

Analysts rate the shares Buy with a $637.36 target [3]. Key risks are $194.1 billion of purchase commitments and a $28.9 billion IRS claim [1]. Our view is neutral: the business is strong, but the price assumes growth that free cash flow has not yet shown.
key_takeaways: Azure momentum should keep revenue compounding, because Azure grew 41% and the $678 billion backlog gives visibility [1].
Free cash flow should only recover once capex growth slows, since capex climbed from $64.6 billion to $115.9 billion while free cash flow fell 6% [1][2].
The valuation looks demanding: the price implies 22% annual growth for ten years against a 6.7% implied return below the 10.1% WACC [3].
Estimate momentum supports the case, with FY2027 EPS consensus up 1.4% over 90 days and 25 analysts raising versus 3 cutting [3].
business_overview:
Microsoft Corporation, founded in 1975, provides cloud services, AI, productivity software, business applications, Windows, devices, video games and online advertising through three segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing [1]. Fiscal 2026 revenue rose 18% to $331.8 billion from $281.7 billion, and net income rose 31% to $133.7 billion [1]. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $214.4 billion, up 27%, making the cloud the core of the group's growth [1]. Sales run through direct enterprise and public-sector channels, a partner network and OEM preinstallation [1].

Productivity and Business Processes grew 16% to $140.0 billion. Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue rose 17% on higher revenue per user from Microsoft 365 Copilot and E5, while seats grew 6% on small and medium business and frontline offerings [1]. Dynamics 365 revenue grew 18% and LinkedIn revenue rose 11% [1]. Microsoft 365 Consumer cloud revenue grew 28%, although the consumer subscriber count was removed as a reported metric in fiscal 2026 [1].

Intelligent Cloud was the growth engine, with revenue up 30% to $137.8 billion. Azure and other cloud services grew 41% across all workloads, while on-premises server products rose only 1% as customers moved to cloud [1]. Management cites three economies of scale: lower unit costs in large datacenters, higher utilization from aggregated demand, and lower maintenance labor from multi-tenancy [1]. Commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678 billion, up 84%, giving visibility on future revenue [1].

More Personal Computing revenue fell 1% to $54.1 billion, as XBOX revenue dropped 7%, with hardware down 29% and content and services down 5% [1]. Search advertising grew 9%, or 12% excluding traffic acquisition costs [1]. Strategic priorities include the OpenAI partnership, extended in October 2025 and April 2026, along with Azure AI Foundry and custom silicon [1]. Capital returns remain large: $16.7 billion of buybacks in fiscal 2026, leaving $40.6 billion of the $60 billion program, and $27.0 billion of dividends declared [1]. Consensus carries a Buy rating and a mean target of $637.36, dated after the 10-K [3].
market_position:
The 10-K does not disclose revenue by geography, name major customers or give market share figures, so these points cannot be assessed from the filing [1]. The filing does show that U.S. income before taxes was $103.6 billion against $62.3 billion from foreign operations, so the earnings base remains weighted toward the home market [1]. Government contracts are a substantial revenue source, and some can be terminated without cause or are subject to periodic funding approval [1]. That adds a policy-linked element to revenue that commercial figures alone do not show [1].

Within its end markets, Microsoft's position rests on breadth rather than a single product. Productivity software, cloud infrastructure, business applications and consumer platforms feed one revenue base, and management says its hybrid deployment options and global scale give it an edge over competitors [1]. Azure growth of 41% and Microsoft 365 commercial seat growth of 6% suggest demand is widening as well as deepening [1]. Consensus expects FY2027 revenue of $396.0 billion, up 19.3%, which would extend this position [3].

The OpenAI relationship is a further element of position. The filing says Microsoft holds rights to OpenAI intellectual property for its products, and the partnership was extended in October 2025 and April 2026 [1]. OpenAI gains added $0.67 per share in fiscal 2026, so the stake is also a source of reported earnings, which is why adjusted EPS is the cleaner comparison [1]. Partner dependence is a risk as well: the filing names some strategic partners as significant Azure customers whose expected demand may not materialise [1].

Classification: established scale leader. On revenue and market value, Microsoft ranks among the largest companies in the peer set. The peer screen gives a market capitalisation of $3,657 billion, close to Alphabet's $3,468 billion and roughly ten times Oracle's $354 billion [2]. Its leadership is one of scale and breadth rather than a challenger position. Because the filing gives no market share data, the classification is qualitative [1][2].
operating_results:
Revenue rose 18% to $331.8 billion in fiscal 2026, and net income rose 31% to $133.7 billion [1]. Cost of revenue grew 21%, faster than revenue, which cut gross margin to 67.9% from 68.8% as AI infrastructure spending rose [1]. Operating expenses grew only 7%, so operating margin widened to 46.8% from 45.6% [1]. Diluted EPS rose to $17.95 from $13.64 [1].

OpenAI gains contributed $0.67 per share; excluding them, adjusted EPS grew 22% to $17.28, the more relevant base for the trend [1]. Consensus FY2027 EPS is $20.03, with estimates up 1.4% over 90 days and 25 analysts raising versus 3 cutting in the past 30 days [3]. Recent quarters beat estimates: EPS of $4.74 in the June 2026 quarter was 11.8% above consensus, and the September 2026 quarter beat by 3.6% [3]. The consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.

Segment results show where the margin pressure sits. Productivity and Business Processes operating income rose 20% to $83.9 billion. Intelligent Cloud operating income rose 28% to $57.0 billion even as its cost of revenue rose 44% to $57.9 billion, lowering segment gross margin to about 58.0% from 62.2% (derived) [1]. The company ties this to AI investment and the mix shift toward Azure, partly offset by efficiency gains [1]. More Personal Computing operating income rose 2% to $14.4 billion despite a 1% revenue decline [1].

Cash generation lagged earnings. Operating cash flow rose 34% to $182.9 billion, but capital expenditure climbed from $64.6 billion to $115.9 billion, so free cash flow fell 6% to $67.0 billion [1][2]. Investing outflows reached $139.5 billion, and financing outflows of $52.5 billion covered dividends of $26.4 billion and buybacks of $22.3 billion [1]. Cash and short-term investments fell to $76.7 billion from $94.6 billion, total debt to $56.8 billion from $60.6 billion, and the current ratio to 1.23 from 1.35 [1][2]. Equity rose 29% to $442.4 billion, lowering debt to equity to 0.13 [1]. Trailing free cash flow of $60.0 billion at 30 September 2026, dated after the 10-K, shows the decline has not yet reversed [2].
risk_assessment:
The filing identifies three top risks [1]. The first is the return on the AI and cloud build-out. Microsoft invests in advance of fully developed revenue streams, and it warns that slower adoption could leave infrastructure underutilized and lead to impairments [1]. Purchase commitments of $194.1 billion, mainly for datacenters, and lease obligations of $443.5 billion add fixed claims on future cash flow [1]. Power constraints and semiconductor shortages could also delay capacity and push revenue out [1]. Free cash flow of $67.0 billion, down 6%, leaves less room for error if returns lag [2].

The second risk is cybersecurity. The filing describes a nation-state attack that began in late November 2023, when a password spray compromised a legacy test account and then reached Microsoft email and some source code repositories [1]. The filing says the incident has harmed reputation and customer relationships, but it does not quantify the cost [1]. Liability limits in licence agreements may not withstand legal challenges, and security spending could reduce operating margins [1].

The third risk is tax and legal exposure. The IRS seeks an additional $28.9 billion plus penalties and interest for tax years 2004 to 2013, centred on intercompany transfer pricing, and the filing says the outcome may differ from amounts recorded [1]. Under accounting rules, a charge could land in a single period once an adverse outcome becomes probable and reasonably estimable [1]. Balance-sheet indicators are less worrying: the Altman Z-score of 8.79 is in the safe zone, and the Beneish M-score of -2.62 gives no manipulation warning [2]. Analysts are still raising estimates, with 25 raising and 3 cutting EPS in the last 30 days [3].

The risks are connected. An AI-related security incident affecting a major customer would touch all three, and the timing of any tax charge is hard to predict. The next test is whether AI revenue grows fast enough to cover the capital already committed [1][2].
competitors_analysis:
Microsoft's margins are the strongest in the four-company set (Alphabet, Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft) for most years shown [1]. Its 2026 EBITDA margin of 62.5% is the highest in the table, against Oracle's 49.7% [2]. Gross margin is 67.9%, above Alphabet's 59.7% and Amazon's 50.3%, though below Oracle's 2025 level of 70.5% [2]. Microsoft's ROIC of 28.2% in 2026 is well above Oracle's 12.6 to 14.2% range, but Alphabet has held a higher ROIC than Microsoft since 2024 (28.7% against 26.8% in 2025) [2].

Cash conversion is the weak spot. FCF conversion fell from 0.84 in 2024 to 0.50 in 2026, and free cash flow fell in both 2025 and 2026 [2]. Alphabet's conversion also declined, from 1.0 in 2022 to 0.55 in 2025, so the pressure is shared across the group rather than unique to Microsoft [2]. Microsoft's 2025 revenue growth of 14.9% was level with Alphabet's 15.1%, and its 2026 growth of 17.8% led Oracle's 17.3% [2].

Valuation is the open question. Microsoft's EV/EBITDA was the highest in the group from 2023 to 2025, but it fell to 13.5 in 2026, well below Oracle's 23.2 [2]. The table does not show whether the fall came from a lower enterprise value or a higher EBITDA base [2]. The consensus view is more constructive: Buy rating, $637.36 target, and a forward P/E of 24.6x on FY2027 EPS [3]. These figures are dated after the 10-K.

Peer selection: Alphabet and Amazon were chosen first because both combine hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure with large advertising or commerce franchises, the same mix as Microsoft's cloud and search businesses [2]. Oracle was chosen as the closest pure-play enterprise cloud infrastructure competitor, though it is only 0.2x Microsoft's revenue [2].

investment_theses.signpost: Azure growth at or above 30% in the Q2 FY2027 results (January 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Azure growth below 25% in any FY2027 quarter, or backlog growth falling well below revenue growth.
